title: A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control
authors: Rahul Golder, Bimol Nath Roy, MM Faruque Hasan
abstract: Physics-constrained machine learning (PCML) integrates domain knowledge, first-principles, and physical constraints into AI/ML models. In this work, we present a step-by-step tutorial of a modular PCML framework, KKT-HardNet, and illustrate how it could be used for hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization and model predictive control in a single platform. KKT-HardNet combines fast inference capabilities of neural networks with guaranteed satisfaction of algebraic constraints through differential projection. It can handle heterogeneous data and enforce both linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints. The modular design supports custom neural-network backbones and user-defined projection mechanisms for PCML. To enable efficient end-to-end training, KKT-HardNet exploits implicit function theorem to backpropagate through the projection layer. This avoids computationally expensive automatic differentiation. This work also introduces an exact reduced-order Fischer-Burmeister reformulation and a primal-dual interior-point method as an alternative projection solve strategy. We also provide a diverse set of benchmarking problems for PCML in engineering applications. KKT-HardNet achieves orders of magnitude better performance in terms of both constraint satisfaction and inference time. The KKT-HardNet code and the benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/souls-tamu/kkt-hardnet .

infographic.key_insight: KKT-HardNet combines neural-network inference with a differentiable projection layer to enforce algebraic physical constraints in physics-constrained machine learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its modular framework supports hybrid modeling, process simulation, optimization, and model predictive control within one platform.
method: Project neural-network outputs to satisfy linear and nonlinear equality and inequality constraints.
Use implicit-function-theorem gradients for end-to-end training through the projection layer.
Support custom backbones and projection mechanisms, including reduced-order Fischer–Burmeister reformulation and primal-dual interior-point solving.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across engineering benchmarks, the abstract reports orders-of-magnitude improvements in constraint satisfaction and inference time; code and benchmark datasets are publicly available.
infographic.watch_item: Practical constraint enforcement depends on projection-solver convergence and numerical tolerances, which are not detailed in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A Tutorial on Physics Constrained Machine Learning for Hybrid Modeling, Optimization, and Control

title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators
authors: Aaditya Prasad, Steven W. Flavell, Brian DePasquale
abstract: State inference and parameter learning for nonlinear filters is a core computation for scientific machine learning with varied applications in engineering and neuroscience. The unnormalized filtering distribution is governed by the Zakai equation, a stochastic partial differential equation (SPDE) that combines the forward Kolmogorov operator (known as the Fokker-Planck equation) with observed likelihood updates. Although solving these high-dimensional SPDEs is often impossible analytically and intractable numerically, advances in operator learning and physics-informed machine learning have made it feasible. Harnessing these advances, we introduce the Zakai Equation Neural Operator (ZENO), a model that optimizes a neural operator against a Zakai Equation based physics-informed loss to approximate the exact unnormalized filtering distribution for latent stochastic dynamical systems. We use this ZENO-inferred posterior distribution in an expectation-maximization (EM) framework to perform parameter learning and state inference. We demonstrate ZENO's ability to accurately infer the posterior distribution and learn its corresponding SDE parameters in three simulated stochastic dynamical systems (Double-Well bistable system, Van Der Pol (VDP) oscillator, and Lorenz system) and compare its performance against established methods for latent SDE inference and learning. We show that ZENO recovers previously observed limit cycles representing forward and backward locomotion from a whole-brain imaging dataset of immobilized \textit{C. elegans} nematodes. ZENO is a novel approach to the problem of nonlinear filtering and dynamical inference through the lens of partial differential equations and operator theory.

infographic.key_insight: ZENO learns a neural operator constrained by the Zakai equation to approximate unnormalized filtering distributions for nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports hidden-state inference and dynamical parameter learning from noisy observations, with potential applications in engineering and neuroscience.
method: Train a neural operator using a Zakai-equation-based physics-informed loss.
Approximate the unnormalized filtering distribution of latent stochastic dynamics.
Use the inferred distribution in expectation-maximization for parameter learning and state inference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers simulated Double-Well, Van der Pol, and Lorenz systems with comparisons to established methods, plus recovery of locomotion-related limit cycles from immobilized C. elegans whole-brain imaging.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify computational cost or establish scalability to substantially higher-dimensional latent systems.
infographic.paper_title: ZENO: Nonlinear filtering with Zakai Equation Neural Operators

title: Iterative Behavioral Identification for Covert Misappropriation Attacks
authors: Victor Mattos, Amit Bhaya, Daniel Sadoc Menasche, Alan O. de Sá
abstract: We present a data-driven, three-phase framework for covert misappropriation attacks on closed-loop networked control systems. A man-in-the-middle (MITM) adversary, with access only to intercepted input-output data, incrementally identifies the plant's behavioral subspace while maintaining stealth under an infinity-norm intrusion-detection system (IDS). Phase 1 collects an initial rank-deficient Hankel matrix using a low-amplitude probing signal that satisfies an analytical stealth bound. Phase 2 adapts online rank-increasing experiment design to the closed-loop setting, using causal predictor-based masking to limit IDS residuals while the Hankel rank grows from 1 to the full behavioral rank n + mL in exactly n + mL - 1 steps. We show that the identified subspaces are strictly nested and that the projection error of any desired trajectory decreases monotonically, strictly so almost surely at each rank increase. Phase 3 employs the final Hankel matrix in a DeePC-style optimization to synthesize a covert attack that tracks an arbitrary reference while respecting the IDS constraint. Simulations on a DC motor with PI control demonstrate full-rank identification and stealthy tracking. Stealth is guaranteed analytically in Phases 1 and 3 and is numerically supported in Phase 2. The method is model-free and assumes noise-free LTI dynamics.

infographic.key_insight: A model-free MITM adversary can progressively identify a closed-loop plant from intercepted input-output data and use the resulting behavioral model to synthesize covert reference-tracking attacks.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework exposes how residual-based intrusion detection can miss incremental system identification and subsequent manipulation of networked control systems.
method: Collect an initial rank-deficient Hankel matrix using low-amplitude probing within an analytical stealth bound.
Use rank-increasing experiments and causal predictor-based masking to reach behavioral rank n + mL in exactly n + mL − 1 steps.
Solve a DeePC-style optimization to track a desired reference while respecting the IDS constraint.
infographic.evidence_signal: DC motor simulations with PI control demonstrate full-rank identification and stealthy tracking; stealth is analytically guaranteed in Phases 1 and 3 but supported only numerically in Phase 2.
infographic.watch_item: The method assumes noise-free LTI dynamics, leaving robustness to measurement noise and model changes unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Iterative Behavioral Identification for Covert Misappropriation Attacks

title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
authors: Yves Delley, John Coller, Zachary Cutts, Alexander Daryin, Mathias Bellaiche, Jun W. Kim
abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.

infographic.key_insight: VERID is a persistent semantic digital twin that connects AI agents’ experimental plans to laboratory execution and supports iterative in-silico self-play.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A queryable, stateful laboratory model can help automation systems validate protocols, recover from execution errors, and preserve traceable experimental records.
method: Expose laboratory state through queryable semantic introspection.
Validate protocols with time-compressed simulation using discrete accounting.
Persist multimodal execution traces and provide a framework for safe execution.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures demonstrate pre-emptive protocol-error detection, stateful mid-run recovery, and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to dye-and-water studies; transfer to complex biochemical workflows and broader physical variability remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories

title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations
authors: Sadra Emami, Benjamin Weigell, Mohammad Reza Mousavi, Gunel Jahangirova, Hugo Araujo, Bernhard Bauer
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to optimize code for performance. This practice often assumes that improvements in execution speed naturally translate into overall lower energy consumption. We challenge this assumption empirically by measuring whether performance-optimized code produced by LLM self-refinement pipelines is also energy-efficient relative to canonical human reference solutions, and whether the energy cost of the optimization process can be offset by subsequent execution-time savings. We evaluate 11 open-source models across four decoding configurations on all 1,000 problems of EffiBench, a state-of-the-art performance benchmark, while collecting per-process, hardware-level energy measurements throughout. Inference energy spans 0.79 to 8.68 MJ across model-variant pairs, which is roughly equivalent to the energy of 250 to 2800 GPT-4.1 queries. Limiting the maximum number of output tokens has the largest impact, reducing energy use by up to 69% compared to the default configuration. On the execution side, 42 of 44 configurations produce code that consumes more energy per problem than the canonical human reference, with overheads ranging from +4% to +886%. The two exceptions achieve only marginal gains, with break-even points on the order of 10^6 to 10^7 executions. Mixture-of-Experts architectures consume substantially less inference energy than equivalently-sized dense models without sacrificing correctness, making architectural choice a more consequential sustainability lever than decoding parameters. Performance optimization and energy efficiency are not always aligned goals: LLM self-refinement consistently produces faster-seeking but energy-heavier code relative to what a human engineer would write. All artifacts are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23598170.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-driven performance optimization rarely reduced execution energy relative to human reference code, while adding substantial inference energy costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Measure optimization and execution energy together, and prioritize model architecture and output-token limits rather than assuming faster code is greener.
method: Evaluate 11 open-source LLMs under four decoding configurations on all 1,000 EffiBench problems.
Collect per-process, hardware-level energy measurements during iterative code optimization and execution.
Compare generated code with canonical human references and estimate energy break-even points.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 44 configurations, 42 produced code using 4%–886% more execution energy than human references; the two energy-saving configurations required roughly 10^6–10^7 executions to offset optimization costs.
infographic.watch_item: Results are specific to the evaluated benchmark, models, and measurement setup; assess energy savings on deployment workloads before adopting self-refinement.
infographic.paper_title: Green Code or Costly Code? Evaluating the Energy Costs of Iterative LLM-Based Code Optimizations

title: Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations
authors: Anouar Imel, Jin Qi
abstract: In LLM-agent opinion simulations, each agent reports the probability that a claim is true after seeing its own previous probability and the probabilities reported by its neighbors, and that number becomes its state in the next round. If the number describes the agent's position rather than the sentence it was shown, then rewriting the claim as its complement and replacing every probability p with 1 - p should return the complementary answer, so the two reports should sum to one. We test this with three small open models: Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B and Gemma-3-4B. On 2,304 agent states taken from a running network simulation, Qwen's paired reports sum to 1.18 on average, and on 48 real fact-checking claims from AVeriTeC they again exceed one. A controlled benchmark of 24 worlds, each with exactly two possible outcomes, shows the same failure in all three models. The discrepancy is two to ten times larger than the change produced by a same-meaning paraphrase, and it persists under repeated sampling and across peer group sizes and report strengths. When the reports are fed back into two populations that start from complementary states, the populations do not remain mirror images: their divergence is positive after five rounds for every model. Averaging each answer with the complement of its paired answer restores consistency by construction and lowers Brier loss averaged over the two wordings, but at the final round it beats the better of the two original wordings for only one of the three models. A schedule-by-targeting experiment on the same model gives a small, stable interaction because such sweeps keep the claim wording fixed. Consistency under rewording therefore needs its own test before simulated probabilities are read as beliefs

infographic.key_insight: LLM-agent probability reports can violate complement consistency: a claim and its opposite do not reliably receive probabilities that sum to one.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Validate consistency under complementary wording before interpreting simulated agent probabilities as beliefs or using them in iterative network simulations.
method: Pair each claim with its complement, replacing prior and neighbor probabilities p with 1 − p.
Evaluate Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Gemma-3-4B using simulation states, fact-checking claims, and controlled two-outcome worlds.
Track complementary populations over repeated rounds and test a paired-answer averaging correction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2,304 simulation states, Qwen’s paired reports averaged 1.18 in total; controlled tests found failures in all three models, with discrepancies 2–10 times larger than same-meaning paraphrase effects.
infographic.watch_item: Paired-answer averaging enforces consistency and lowers Brier loss averaged across wordings, but beats the better original wording at the final round for only one of three models.
infographic.paper_title: Do "True" and "False" Add Up to One? Complement Consistency in LLM-Agent Opinion Simulations

title: SceneBloom: Agentic Indoor Environment Generation with Realistic and Diverse Layouts for Embodied Learning
authors: Yuhan Liu, Lianhui Qin, Shenji Wan
abstract: Training generalizable embodied agents requires realistic, varied, and simulation-ready indoor environments. Language-guided methods support semantic planning and object-level reasoning, but precise spatial grounding remains difficult. Visual generative models offer rich priors over plausible arrangements, yet their outputs require geometric reasoning to become physically valid 3D scenes. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that combines visual layout sampling with contract-guided 3D compilation. A hierarchical sampler uses diffusion priors to generate furniture arrangements within functional zones. A compiler then uses relations extracted from each proposal to guide geometric fitting and local pose correction. Across five room types, SceneBloom attains the highest visual quality and physical stability among the compared methods and is the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out-of-bounds objects. Its layouts are also closer to the distribution of real rooms than those of all compared baselines. Object navigation policies trained in these realistic scenes achieve a higher success rate in held-out real scans than those trained on an equal number of real training scans. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/scenebloom.

infographic.key_insight: SceneBloom combines visual layout generation with geometry-aware 3D compilation to produce realistic, diverse indoor scenes for embodied learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Simulation-ready layouts can improve object-navigation transfer to real environments while reducing reliance on real training scans.
method: Sample furniture arrangements within functional zones using hierarchical diffusion priors.
Extract spatial relations from proposals to guide contract-based 3D compilation.
Fit geometry and correct object poses locally.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five room types, SceneBloom reports the best visual quality and physical stability among compared methods, no detected mesh collisions or out-of-bounds objects, and higher held-out real-scan navigation success than training on an equal number of real scans.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify performance gains or compilation costs, leaving practical scalability uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: SceneBloom: Agentic Indoor Environment Generation with Realistic and Diverse Layouts for Embodied Learning

title: On the Identifiability of Hybrid Deep Generative Models: Meta-Learning as a Solution
authors: Yubo Ye, Maryam Toloubidokhti, Sumeet Vadhavkar, Xiajun Jiang, Huafeng Liu, Linwei Wang
abstract: The interest in leveraging physics-based inductive bias in deep learning has resulted in recent development of hybrid deep generative models (hybrid-DGMs) that integrate known physics-based mathematical expressions in neural generative models. To identify these hybrid-DGMs requires inferring parameters of the physics-based component along with their neural component. The identifiability of these hybrid-DGMs, however, has not yet been theoretically probed or established. How does the existing theory of the un-identifiability of general DGMs apply to hybrid-DGMs? What may be an effective approach to construct a hybrid-DGM with theoretically-proven identifiability? This paper provides the first theoretical probe into the identifiability of hybrid-DGMs, and presents meta-learning as a novel solution to construct identifiable hybrid-DGMs. On synthetic and real-data benchmarks, we provide strong empirical evidence for the un-identifiability of existing hybrid-DGMs using unconditional priors, and strong identifiability results of the presented meta-formulations of hybrid-DGMs. Code is available at https://github.com/GoForIt-YYB/Meta-Hybrid-VAE.

infographic.key_insight: Embedding known physics in deep generative models does not by itself ensure identifiability; the paper presents meta-learning formulations with theoretical identifiability guarantees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Identifiable hybrid models can make inferred physical parameters more trustworthy when combining mechanistic equations with neural generative components.
method: Analyze identifiability when physical and neural parameters are inferred jointly.
Construct meta-learning formulations of hybrid deep generative models.
Compare meta-formulations with existing hybrid models using unconditional priors.
infographic.evidence_signal: Synthetic and real-data benchmarks provide strong empirical evidence of non-identifiability in existing unconditional-prior models and identifiability in the proposed meta-formulations.
infographic.watch_item: Check the theorem assumptions and meta-learning data requirements before applying the identifiability guarantees to a new engineering system.
infographic.paper_title: On the Identifiability of Hybrid Deep Generative Models: Meta-Learning as a Solution

title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yijing Ke, Tianle Cai, Ruosong Wang
abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.

infographic.key_insight: Aligning selected training-side rounding locations with inference stabilizes BF16 LLM reinforcement learning without matching the entire execution stack.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Targeted precision handling can prevent training collapse while leaving the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.
method: Align rounding locations in RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm.
Retain selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs.
Evaluate full three-region alignment and RoPE-path alignment alone.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four Qwen-family models, three-region alignment prevented the collapse seen with default BF16; RoPE-path alignment alone also sufficed in the studied runs.
infographic.watch_item: RoPE-only sufficiency is established only for the studied runs, and numerical discrepancies remain after alignment.
infographic.paper_title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning

title: Yalda-Embedding: Open Development of a Competitive Persian Retrieval Model
authors: Yalda Taheri, Mohammad Hassan Heydari, Armon Rasooli
abstract: Despite advances in multilingual text representations, effective dense retrieval for Persian remains constrained by the limited availability of language-specific training resources and compact embedding models. We present Yalda Embedding, a 595.8-million-parameter Persian retrieval model adapted from Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B using more than one million query-document pairs. On eight Persian retrieval tasks from FaMTEB, the model achieves the highest macro-average among the evaluated 0.6B models, scoring 0.5488 and outperforming Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and F2LLM-v2-0.6B on every task. It also approaches Qwen3-Embedding-4B, winning on four tasks, tying on one, and trailing by 0.0075 in macro-average. An incremental ablation study examines contrastive batch size, optimization stabilization, and relational knowledge distillation from F2LLM-v2-8B. Under the one-epoch training setup, contrastive fine-tuning alone yields a modest mean improvement over initialization and regressions on two tasks. The final distilled configuration improves all eight tasks over the non-distilled model, raising the mean from 0.4813 to 0.5488 without increasing inference-time model size. These gains include hard-negative evaluation tasks despite training without explicitly mined or supplied hard negatives. We release model weights, training and evaluation code, the pairwise dataset, and its teacher-embedded counterpart, enabling inspection of data composition and training procedures, independent evaluation, and reuse without repeating expensive teacher inference.

infographic.key_insight: Yalda-Embedding improves compact Persian retrieval through relational knowledge distillation, achieving the highest macro-average among evaluated 0.6B models without increasing inference-time model size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Released weights, code, training pairs, and teacher embeddings support reproducible Persian retrieval development while avoiding repeated teacher-inference costs.
method: Adapt Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B using over one million Persian query-document pairs.
Study contrastive batch size and optimization stabilization through incremental ablations.
Apply relational knowledge distillation from F2LLM-v2-8B without explicitly mined or supplied hard negatives.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across eight FaMTEB Persian retrieval tasks, distillation raises the macro-average from 0.4813 to 0.5488, improving every task over the non-distilled model and finishing 0.0075 behind Qwen3-Embedding-4B.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to eight Persian retrieval benchmarks and a one-epoch training setup; broader domain generalization remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Yalda-Embedding: Open Development of a Competitive Persian Retrieval Model

title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks
authors: Takeru Hasegawa, Naoto Mitsume, Shota Deguchi, Mitsuteru Asai, Tetsuya Kanagawa
abstract: Interactions between ultrasound and microbubbles underlie a range of biomedical and industrial applications, yet predicting how the physical parameters of the medium and bubbles govern nonlinear wave propagation remains difficult. This study proposes a parameter estimation framework that combines a Korteweg-de Vries-Burgers (KdVB) equation, describing weakly nonlinear wave propagation in a bubbly liquid, with a physics-informed neural network (PINN). The contributions are threefold. First, the PINN reproduces the reference solution of the governing equation in the forward problem, with a near-zero prediction error at the initial time that confirms the initial condition is enforced exactly as intended. Second, prior to inverse estimation, a sensitivity analysis is introduced that quantifies, at both the coefficient and solution levels, how each of eight physical parameters influences the KdVB equation, allowing the expected difficulty of estimating each parameter to be assessed in advance. Third, based on this assessment, single-parameter inverse estimation is performed for seven of the eight parameters using the PINN. Liquid viscosity, bubble initial radius, liquid density, sound speed, and liquid pressure are estimated with errors of 0.8-2.1%, the polytropic exponent converges only partially, and the surface tension coefficient cannot be estimated at all, consistent with the sensitivity analysis. These results establish a general framework for identifying and estimating the physical parameters governing nonlinear wave propagation in bubbly liquids from observed waveform data.

infographic.key_insight: Sensitivity analysis helps anticipate which bubbly-liquid parameters a physics-informed neural network can recover from nonlinear waveforms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could guide parameter estimation for ultrasound–microbubble systems by identifying informative parameters before inverse modeling.
method: Model weakly nonlinear wave propagation with the Korteweg–de Vries–Burgers equation.
Assess eight physical parameters through coefficient- and solution-level sensitivity analysis.
Validate the PINN forward solution, then estimate seven parameters individually.
infographic.evidence_signal: The PINN reproduced the reference solution and estimated viscosity, initial bubble radius, density, sound speed, and pressure with 0.8–2.1% errors; the polytropic exponent converged partially, while surface tension estimation failed.
infographic.watch_item: Single-parameter results do not establish reliable simultaneous estimation or robustness to noisy experimental waveforms.
infographic.paper_title: Sensitivity-Guided Parameter Estimation of Bubbly Liquid via a Nonlinear Wave Equation and Physics-InformedNeuralNetworks

title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
authors: Federico Lucca
abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, what it is, whether it is urgent, whether to draft a reply, create a task, or ignore it. Their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We present Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent in daily use, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, pre-registered hypotheses, human labels in the agent's review loop) that yields ground truth before any training. On 739 real Italian/English emails labelled by the owner (231 unbiased, 500 adversarially sampled), we compare nine systems under thread-grouped cross-validation: the production keyword rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble), a hosted decision model (Nimble v4-max), and hosted generative LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma 4 26B/31B). Four results. The production rules score 28% on message type against a 58% majority class: the field shown most prominently carried no information. With ~200 labels, logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90), though it never predicts the two rarest classes and is statistically tied with Gemma 4 on type; few-shot prompting does not close the gap. The sender's relationship (client, supplier, service) is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy where the contact has been seen, and is not inferable from a single message by any model: it belongs in the contact graph, not the prompt. Finally, accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the most accurate system most often ignores emails needing action (18% vs 4% for the best LLM); a cost-chosen threshold on its noise probability halves that rate and makes it the cheapest system.

infographic.key_insight: Measure before training: a simple logistic-regression baseline led field-level accuracy, but action-aware thresholding was needed to reduce costly missed emails.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Evaluate downstream action costs, tune decision thresholds, and store sender relationships in a contact graph rather than relying on single-message inference.
method: Establish human ground truth using stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, and pre-registered hypotheses.
Compare nine rule-based, classical, typed-decision, and generative systems with thread-grouped cross-validation.
Compose predictions into inbox actions and select a noise threshold based on error costs.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 739 owner-labelled Italian/English emails, including 231 unbiased and 500 adversarially sampled examples, logistic regression achieved 0.79 type accuracy but ignored 18% of emails needing action versus 4% for the best LLM; threshold tuning halved its miss rate.
infographic.watch_item: Results come from one owner's inbox, and the strongest accuracy baseline never predicted the two rarest classes, limiting conclusions about generalization and rare-event reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox

title: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Step Transition Predictions: A Bellman Theory
authors: Chenbei Lu, Zaiwei Chen, Tongxin Li, Chenye Wu, Adam Wierman
abstract: Multi-step predictions of future transition realizations can improve reinforcement learning, but their value remains difficult to quantify. Directly including these predictions in the state can lead to exponential state-space growth, making direct dynamic programming computationally expensive. We study discounted finite MDPs under a block-feedback protocol: at the start of each K-period block, the decision maker observes $K$-step probabilistic transition predictions for a subset of actions and adapts decisions to observed states within the block. We show that the optimal value satisfies a Bayesian Bellman equation on the original state space. This representation reveals that predictive information creates value by recursively changing the local order of maximization and expectation in the Bellman expansion. We formalize this effect through a Bellman--Jensen analysis and quantify the effects of prediction horizon, error, action coverage, and within-block feedback. We propose block-feedback Bayesian offline learning with online adaptation (BF--BOLA), a model-based algorithm for learning near-optimal policies, and establish upper and lower sample-complexity bounds that match up to logarithmic factors in the stated regimes. The results show that predictions can reduce transition learning to uncovered rows and that learning a near-optimal policy can require fewer prediction samples than estimating the Bayesian value function.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-step transition predictions improve decision-making through a Bayesian Bellman equation on the original state space, avoiding exponential state augmentation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predictive information can reduce transition-learning needs to uncovered state–action rows while supporting adaptive decisions within each prediction block.
method: Model discounted finite MDPs with K-step probabilistic predictions for a subset of actions and within-block state feedback.
Use Bellman–Jensen analysis to quantify effects of prediction horizon, error, action coverage, and feedback.
Apply BF–BOLA: block-feedback Bayesian offline learning with online adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical upper and lower sample-complexity bounds matching up to logarithmic factors in stated regimes, but no empirical evaluation.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees concern a specific finite-MDP block-feedback protocol; practical deployment must account for prediction error and incomplete action coverage.
infographic.paper_title: Reinforcement Learning with Multi-Step Transition Predictions: A Bellman Theory

title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding
authors: Nilesh Prasad Pandey, Jangseon Park, Jason Kong, Onat Gungor, Tajana Rosing
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling.

infographic.key_insight: Recent rollouts for the same prompt provide reusable n-gram drafts that accelerate RL post-training without an auxiliary model while preserving the rollout distribution through target-model verification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: NgramRL targets the autoregressive rollout bottleneck, which can exceed 70% of training time, without requiring drafter training or persistent GPU-resident drafter state.
method: Build per-prompt n-gram draft caches from bounded recent rollout histories.
Verify drafts with the target model to preserve the rollout distribution.
Adaptively prefetch likely verification outcomes under a candidate budget, falling back to sequential lookup for uncovered outcomes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two model families and three workloads, warm-cache NgramRL commits 3.60–7.77 tokens per target forward; on Spider, prefetching delivers 1.38× measured rollout throughput over synchronous NgramRL.
infographic.watch_item: Reported token-efficiency gains are from the warm-cache regime; cold starts or limited repetition across rollouts may reduce benefits.
infographic.paper_title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding

title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
authors: Kamillo Ferry, Anthea Monod, Keisuke Yano
abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. We characterize this geometry locally through observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. The global learning complexity need not be determined at a ground-truth parameter, as singularities on another rank stratum can dominate. We also introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT. Experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation.

infographic.key_insight: LoRA’s learning complexity depends on which low-rank updates the pretrained network can statistically distinguish, not simply on its trainable parameter count.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Layer-specific activation and gradient geometry can help assess LoRA’s effective complexity beyond adapter rank or parameter budget.
method: Locally linearize LoRA as low-rank trace regression with a forward-backward covariance.
Analyze singular geometry using observable tangent directions and affine sections of determinantal varieties.
Estimate the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) with a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on multilayer perceptrons and transformers show strongly layer-dependent geometry; ambient covariance degeneracy does not necessarily imply degeneracy along relevant low-rank directions.
infographic.watch_item: The local linearization is an approximation, and global learning complexity can be dominated by singularities away from the ground-truth rank stratum.
infographic.paper_title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation

title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows
authors: Tirthankar De, Sayantan Auddy, Ramit Dey, Shantanu Basu
abstract: Molecular clouds exhibit complex, multi-scale dynamics driven by the interplay of turbulence, self-gravity, and gas pressure. Modelling these systems with conventional grid-based methods becomes increasingly expensive as spatial resolution and dimensionality increase. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) offer a mesh-free alternative by incorporating the governing equations directly into the training objective, but their ability to model realistic turbulent self-gravitating flows remains largely unexplored. We apply PINNs to isothermal molecular clouds initialized with astrophysically motivated turbulent velocity fields, considering subsonic and supersonic evolution in two and three dimensions. We benchmark the predicted density and velocity fields against the finite-volume code Athena++. PINNs accurately recover the global evolution of the flow over multiple free-fall times across turbulent realizations, Mach numbers, and dimensionalities. Their training cost also exhibits weak dependence on spatial resolution, increasing by less than 25% from 128^3 to 1024^3 in our experiments. These results demonstrate that PINNs can model substantially more realistic self-gravitating turbulent flows than previously explored and provide a promising complementary framework for studying these systems.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-Informed Neural Networks recover the global evolution of multidimensional turbulent, self-gravitating molecular clouds while showing weak training-cost dependence on spatial resolution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PINNs offer a promising mesh-free complement to grid-based solvers for computationally demanding self-gravitating flow simulations.
method: Embed governing physics equations in the neural-network training objective.
Model isothermal clouds with astrophysically motivated turbulence in 2D and 3D.
Benchmark predicted density and velocity fields against Athena++ finite-volume simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across turbulent realizations, subsonic and supersonic regimes, and dimensionalities, PINNs accurately recover global evolution over multiple free-fall times; reported training cost rises by less than 25% from 128³ to 1024³.
infographic.watch_item: Global agreement does not establish fidelity to small-scale turbulent structures, and weak training-cost scaling alone does not demonstrate an end-to-end speed advantage over Athena++.
infographic.paper_title: Physics Informed Neural Network for Multi-dimensional Turbulent Self-gravitating Flows

title: CARES: Coverage-Aware Replay Exemplar Selection for Continual Learning
authors: Arundhati S. Shanbhag, Brian B. Moser, Federico Raue, Tobias C. Nauen, Andreas Dengel
abstract: Replay-based Continual Learning mitigates catastrophic forgetting by keeping a buffer of past samples, making buffer composition critical under a fixed memory budget. Recent coreset-based replay methods improve buffer quality using model-derived gradients, losses, or auxiliary optimization, but incur substantial computational overhead as memory is repeatedly updated. We propose CARES, a continual model-optimization-free approach for buffer construction that instead exploits the geometry of a frozen pretrained feature space using class-aware, density-weighted coverage. We evaluate CARES across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings. On Tiny-ImageNet, CARES is 2.3 to 8.8 times faster than existing coreset-based selectors. Although CARES achieves this speedup using no training signal from the continual learner, it ranks among the state of the art across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy streams under online class- and task-incremental settings, outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 7.58 percentage points under class imbalance while also attaining higher average accuracy on Tiny-ImageNet. Code will be released upon publication

infographic.key_insight: CARES selects replay exemplars through class-aware, density-weighted coverage in a frozen pretrained feature space, avoiding continual-learner optimization signals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CARES can reduce replay-buffer selection overhead under fixed memory budgets while maintaining competitive continual-learning accuracy.
method: Represent samples using a frozen pretrained feature extractor.
Select exemplars using class-aware, density-weighted feature-space coverage.
Construct replay buffers without learner gradients, losses, or auxiliary optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across balanced, imbalanced, and label-noisy online class- and task-incremental evaluations, CARES reports 2.3–8.8× faster selection on Tiny-ImageNet and gains of up to 7.58 percentage points over the strongest baseline under class imbalance.
infographic.watch_item: Selection quality may depend on how well the frozen pretrained feature space represents the incoming data; code release is pending publication.
infographic.paper_title: CARES: Coverage-Aware Replay Exemplar Selection for Continual Learning

title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents
authors: Navyansh Mahla, Sashank Vandrangi
abstract: LLM agents need long-term memory that can recover precise and mutually consistent evidence from growing interaction histories, particularly when answers depend on relations among facts rather than isolated semantic matches. Current memory pipelines remain vulnerable at two stages: indexing errors can fragment repeated entities or merge distinct ones, and online retrieval often treats initial similarity scores as final even when the surrounding graph provides evidence for revising them. We introduce ActionRAG, a graph memory architecture that couples cautious indexing with query-time graph retroevaluation. Its indexing pipeline reconciles type labels and applies tiered entity resolution. Given a query, dual-channel entity and triple retrieval forms an initial evidence set and induces a bounded local graph. Query-conditioned receiver-normalized diffusion refines triple scores using local path structure. Seed protection, hub-penalized flux, and triple materialization preserve direct evidence while recovering missed connections. We evaluate ActionRAG on MemoryAgentBench (MAB), which tests accurate retrieval, conflict resolution, long-range understanding, and test-time learning. Across its eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG achieves 55.1 average accuracy, improving over the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points. Under MAB's query-time cost accounting, mean synthesis cost stays below \$0.001 per query on the four reported cost columns, and the sum of separately measured retrieval-side p99 components is 440.7 ms on our consumer Apple Silicon setup.

infographic.key_insight: ActionRAG improves LLM long-term memory by refining retrieved evidence through query-conditioned graph diffusion rather than relying solely on initial similarity scores.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The architecture targets agents that must recover precise, mutually consistent facts and relationships from growing interaction histories.
method: Reconcile type labels and apply tiered entity resolution during indexing.
Retrieve entities and triples through dual channels to construct a bounded local evidence graph.
Refine triple scores with receiver-normalized diffusion, seed protection, hub penalties, and triple materialization.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MemoryAgentBench’s eight deterministic-scoring columns, ActionRAG averages 55.1 accuracy, beating the strongest retrieval-based memory baseline by 5.4 points; mean synthesis cost is below $0.001 per query on four reported cost columns.
infographic.watch_item: The reported 440.7 ms sums separately measured retrieval-side p99 components on consumer Apple Silicon; it is not an end-to-end p99 latency measurement.
infographic.paper_title: ActionRAG: Evidence-Refining Graph Diffusion for Long-Term Memory in LLM Agents

title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials
authors: Zhilong Song, Zijun Pang, Lixue Cheng
abstract: Crystal materials are designed either by screening known crystals for a target property or by generating new crystals with that property. Both routes are judged against public databases of known crystals, but these databases name the same crystal differently. Several materials announced as new by recent generative and autonomous discovery campaigns have since proved to be known phases or close variants of them. The limits of both routes remain unmeasured. Here we probe them by matching the crystals of 55 databases by structure into one self-extending database of 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values, each traced to its source. Only 4.5% of its crystal-property pairs carry a value. To fill the empty pairs, we developed CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer with state-of-the-art accuracy on several tasks of two public benchmarks. Trained on each task, it forms a library of property models whose predictions we release. The reach of forward screening has been underestimated. Known crystals hold tens of thousands of ultra-incompressible candidates without a recorded bulk modulus, and a post hoc audit of synthesis evidence finds among them ReN2, whose bulk modulus was measured at 428 GPa. The novelty claimed for inverse design has been overestimated. At an equal verification budget, a stiffness-conditioned generator returned more stiff hits than screening (100 versus 55), but all contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions. Integrating and completing the databases of known crystals therefore moves the limits of both routes: it widens what screening can reach and sets the reference against which generated crystals are judged new.

infographic.key_insight: Unifying crystal databases expands the reach of screening known materials while exposing overstated novelty in inverse-designed crystals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structure-matched records and property models can help engineers identify overlooked candidates and assess whether generated materials are genuinely new.
method: Match crystal structures across 55 databases into a source-traceable, self-extending database.
Train CGTNet, an equivariant graph transformer, to predict missing material properties.
Audit screening candidates and compare screening with stiffness-conditioned generation at equal verification budgets.
infographic.evidence_signal: The database contains 14.6 million crystals and 131.8 million property values; generation yielded 100 stiff hits versus screening’s 55, but all generated hits contained osmium and 82 repeated recorded compositions.
infographic.watch_item: Only 4.5% of crystal-property pairs have recorded values, so predicted candidates still require validation, and repeated compositions alone do not establish structural duplication.
infographic.paper_title: Probing the limits of forward screening and inverse design of crystal materials

title: Do Language Models Trust Their Own Justifications? A Study on Functional Consistency
authors: Alisson Rosa Pereira, Bruno Iochins Grisci
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely adopted in text classification tasks, where they not only output class predictions but also generate explanations that highlight the tokens deemed most relevant for reaching the predicted label. Yet it remains unclear whether these highlighted elements are behaviorally consistent with the model's own predictions under targeted interventions, which we refer to as functional auto-consistency. While much of the literature evaluates the textual plausibility of such explanations, few studies assess their functional consistency with the model's actual behavior. In this work, we propose an experimental framework based on the principle of auto-consistency: if a model identifies certain tokens as decisive, then isolating, removing, or semantically inverting them should produce systematic and interpretable changes in its predictions. We operationalize this evaluation through sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality metrics, and conduct experiments on IMDB and Steam reviews across both closed-source (GPT-4o-mini) and open-source LLMs (Gemma3, Granite8B, DeepSeek). Results show that GPT-4o-mini follows the expected progression across all metrics, Gemma3 and Granite8B maintain coherence under sufficiency but lose consistency under more demanding interventions, while DeepSeek variants display structural deviations, either failing to preserve sufficiency or overreacting under comprehensiveness and counterfactuality. These findings show that explanation reliability varies across LLM families and scales, with smaller models displaying contradictions and larger ones exhibiting over-sensitivity. By combining sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality, our approach provides a systematic methodology for assessing the functional consistency of LLM self-explanations.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-highlighted evidence does not always align with prediction behavior, and consistency varies across model families and intervention types.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Test model-generated explanations with targeted input interventions before relying on them for classification audits or decision support.
method: Ask models to classify reviews and highlight decisive tokens.
Isolate, remove, or semantically invert highlighted tokens.
Evaluate functional auto-consistency using sufficiency, comprehensiveness, and counterfactuality.
infographic.evidence_signal: On IMDB and Steam reviews, GPT-4o-mini followed expected patterns across all metrics; Gemma3 and Granite8B preserved sufficiency but weakened under harder interventions, while DeepSeek variants showed structural deviations.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports qualitative patterns without numerical effect sizes, leaving the magnitude of model differences unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Do Language Models Trust Their Own Justifications? A Study on Functional Consistency
